props.title: Trouble the Water
props.initialSlug: Survival in the face of disaster.

sections.content: Trouble the Water stands as one of the most powerful Hurricane Katrina documentaries ever made, distinguished by its raw, ground-level footage shot by aspiring rapper Kimberly Rivers Roberts. Unlike media coverage that focused on helicopter views or outside perspectives, this film puts viewers directly in the 9th Ward through Roberts' handheld camera. The documentary echoes the citizen journalism impact of Medium Cool (1969) while following the urgent, immediate style of When the Levees Broke (2006). Roberts' footage captures not just the hurricane, but the systemic failures and institutional racism that amplified the disaster.

sections.content: The film revolutionized disaster documentary storytelling by centering survivor perspectives rather than outside observers. Like The Florida Project (2017) and Chop Shop (2007), it captures marginalized American experiences through an intimate, observational lens. Roberts' amateur footage, rather than being a limitation, provides an unfiltered window into the experience of poor, Black residents abandoned by their government during the crisis.

The documentary's structure brilliantly weaves Roberts' raw hurricane footage with the aftermath of displacement and attempted recovery. This approach influenced later works like Time (2020) and Strong Island (2017), showing how personal archives can illuminate broader systemic issues. The film's exploration of race, class, and government failure creates a devastating portrait of American inequality that remains relevant today. SUBHEAD: Impact on Social Justice Documentary Film

Trouble the Water transformed how documentarians approach disaster coverage and social justice storytelling. Its influence can be seen in films like Welcome to Leith (2015) and Quest (2017), which similarly embed themselves in communities over extended periods to reveal deeper truths. The film's success helped pave the way for more documentaries centering marginalized voices telling their own stories, rather than being subjects of outside observation.
